processing: Ripe pu-erh from the Menghai Tea Factory: wet-piled Yunnan large-leaf tea, blended to a numbered recipe and pressed into cakes. Sellers disagree on the leaf, some saying mostly grade 3 and another an average of grade 5.
harvest_season: Not tied to one picking: factory recipes are blended from stored material.
appearance_dry: A 357 g brown cake of ripe large-leaf tea, as listed by retailers.
appearance_liquor: Dark red-brown, as usual for Menghai ripe pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Soft dark brown leaf, as usual for ripe pu-erh.
taste_profile: Little tasting detail is recorded for this recipe; expect what is typical of Menghai ripe tea, with earth, dark sweetness and a smooth body.

brewing.notes: Standard ripe handling: rinse once and use near-boiling water.

vintage_note: Dayi teas are normally sold by year and batch, and 357 g cakes from 2011 and 2012 are among those listed by retailers. One database records seven ripe productions under 0532, so this is a recurring recipe.
description:
0532 is one of the numbered ripe recipes of the Menghai Tea Factory, the maker behind the Dayi brand. It is less often discussed than 7572 or 7262, and one retailer sells it as among the factory's highest-grade ripe recipes, which is a seller's praise.

As a ripe tea it is piled and fermented before pressing. Informal explanations of Menghai numbers treat the first two digits as the year of the recipe, the third as the main leaf grade and the last, 2, as the Menghai factory. On that reading 0532 would be a 2005 recipe built around grade 3 leaf. A retailer gives the same date and grade, but another seller says grade 5, and neither is a factory statement.

There is not much on record about how it tastes. Expect the usual Menghai ripe profile, and brew it hot after a rinse.

Note the batch code when buying, since it usually tells you the production year.
history:
The Menghai Tea Factory dates to 1940 and was among the first two factories making ripe pu-erh in 1973. It became fully private in 1996 and adopted the Dayi trademark.

Little is documented about 0532 itself. A retailer dates the recipe to 2005, and one database lists seven ripe productions under the number.
